title: 09 - Indian Political Thought

content.text: Syllabus — Indian Political Thought: Dharmashastra, Arthashastra and Buddhist traditions; Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar, M.N. Roy. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 9)

the ancient traditions — Dharmashastra (Manu), Arthashastra (Kautilya) and Buddhist political thought — and the modern thinkers Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar and M.N. Roy.

Manu (dharma, varna), Kautilya (Saptanga, Mandala, Danda-niti, Matsyanyaya), Buddha (MahaSammat, Dhamma), Sir Syed (two-nation theory), Aurobindo (spiritual nationalism, Purna Swaraj), Gandhi (Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya, Trusteeship), Ambedkar (annihilation of caste, social democracy), M.N. Roy (radical humanism).

Gandhi (2020/2019/2016/2015) and Ambedkar (2022/2020/2018/2016/2013) are the highest-yield; also Kautilya’s statecraft (2017/2012/2010/2007), Buddhist ethics (2021), Aurobindo (2017/2016/2014/2013), Sir Syed (2021/2013), Dharma (2020), M.N. Roy.

Q — Explicate the ideological components of Gandhism — Truth/Ahimsa, Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya and Trusteeship — and evaluate his critique of modern Western civilization and his view of the state. (UPSC 2020/2019/2016/2015)
List the building blocks of Gandhi’s thought one by one, then judge his attack on modern civilization and on the state itself.
— the twin foundation: ‘God and truth are inseparable’ and non-violence is ‘not the resort of the weak but the power of the strong’.
(Ahimsa is active love, not cowardly submission — the man who runs away from the blow is not practising it.)
— satya + agraha = ‘soul-force over brute-force through self-suffering’, aimed ‘against the evil, not the evil-doer’.
(The satyagrahi breaks the unjust law openly, accepts the lathi-blow and the jail term without retaliating, so the opponent’s conscience — not his body — is defeated.)
: ‘Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi furnished the method’.

(Not swapping a white ruler for a brown one: it is the village governing itself and the individual mastering his own appetites — ending in Ram Rajya, a near-stateless order of self-governing ‘oceanic circles’.)
, ‘the uplift of all’ through bread labour, with the rich as ‘trustees, not owners’.
(The mill-owner keeps the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers, drawing only what he needs — ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’.)
modern Western civilization is ‘satanic’ and materialist, and the state is ‘a soulless machine’ resting on coercion.
(Railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than civilisation.)
— ends and means are continuous: ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’.
(A freedom won by terror would itself have been an unfree India.)
called him ‘not a philosopher but a strategist… a psychologist’, and his ideas — set out in
, drawing on the Gita, Tolstoy and Ruskin — rest on two inseparable foundations. ‘God and truth are inseparable’, and
is the only means of realising truth: it is ‘not the resort of the weak but the power of the strong’, active love rather than the cowardice of the man who simply runs away from the blow.

(satya + agraha) — ‘soul-force over brute-force through self-suffering’, directed ‘against the evil, not the evil-doer’, and therefore quite distinct from mere passive resistance, which is the weapon of the weak. In practice the satyagrahi disobeys the unjust law openly, invites arrest and absorbs the blow without returning it, converting the opponent by melting his conscience instead of crushing his body.
acknowledged the debt: ‘Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi furnished the method’.

together — political, economic, social and cultural. Merely replacing English rulers by Indian ones would be English rule without the Englishman; genuine Swaraj means the village governing its own affairs through Panchayati Raj and the individual governing his own appetites. Its culmination is

, a stateless society of ‘oceanic circles’ in which the individual is the centre and no circle dominates another. His famous image guards this from parochialism: ‘I do not want my house to be walled in… I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house… but I refuse to be blown off my feet’.
— ‘the uplift of all’ rather than the greatest good of the greatest number — resting on

. Capitalists are ‘trustees, not owners’: the mill-owner retains the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers and for society, drawing only what he genuinely needs, since ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’. This substitutes class cooperation and a change of heart for the Marxist expropriation of the propertied class.

Gandhi condemns modern Western civilization as materialist and ‘satanic’ — it multiplies wants instead of mastering them, and its railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than true civilisation, which he defines as that mode of conduct which points out to man the path of duty. The

is condemned on the same ground: it is ‘a soulless machine’ based on coercion, representing violence in a concentrated and organised form, and it stunts the self-reliance and moral growth of the individual. His ideal is therefore ‘enlightened anarchy’ — government reduced to the minimum as men learn to govern themselves.

Gandhism fuses ethics and politics through the ‘continuity of ends and means’ — ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’, for a freedom won by terror would itself be unfree. Though Trusteeship and Ram Rajya are criticised as impractical and utopian, Gandhi’s non-violent Satyagraha remains his enduring contribution to world politics.
Q — Explain the sources and salient features of ancient Indian political thought, and examine the significance of Dharma in the Dharmashastra (Manu) tradition. (UPSC 2020)
Where ancient Indian thought comes from, what marks it out, and why Dharma is its master-concept.

(Riti does for India what natural law does for the West — a higher order the ruler did not make and cannot unmake.)

(Sant Tukaram: ‘the entire world is a family’ — the individual sits inside kula, jati and society, never against them.)
— ‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’, differing in degree, not in kind.
(Politics is a chapter of ethics here, not the separate autonomous science it becomes in Machiavelli.)

(It is social cement — each varna and ashrama performing its own svadharma keeps the whole edifice standing.)
(‘The big fish eats the small fish’ — anarchy, where strength alone decides.)
Hence the king has ‘divine personality’ but

(‘The lower the varna, the higher the punishment’.)
Ancient Indian (‘Hindu’) political thought derives from

: a standard the ruler neither creates nor can abolish, and against which his commands are measured. Its textual sources are the

Four features stand out. It shows ‘enormous continuity’ of dharma and danda across centuries rather than sharp ruptures. It is
— the individual is always located within family, kula, jati and society, never posed against them as in Western individualism. It is
‘the entire world is a family’ captures the vasudhaiva kutumbakam spirit. But it is also

‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’ — but they differ only in
, for Indian thought treats them not ‘in silos but in a continuum’. Politics is thus a chapter of ethics rather than an autonomous science, unlike the Machiavellian separation of the two. Within the
tradition dharma is the core and danda the periphery; in the Arthashastra the emphasis is exactly reversed.
, the ‘first law-giver’ and Manasputra of Brahma, is the chief exponent of this tradition.
— at once moral, natural and social order — is its master concept: ‘

’, dharma is that which holds life on earth. It works as social cement, each varna and each ashrama discharging its own svadharma so that the whole edifice stands; and it is also the source of the king’s obligations, since Raj Dharma binds him as tightly as it binds the subject.
The significance of dharma is shown negatively by what follows its absence:

— literally the law of the fish, where ‘the big fish eats the small fish’ and strength alone decides, the Indian equivalent of the Hobbesian state of nature. Kingship exists precisely to prevent this. Yet although the king possesses a ‘divine personality’, he has

Dharma is therefore the master concept of the ancient Indian polity — it simultaneously legitimises kingship and limits it, anticipating constitutionalism without a constitution. Yet the same tradition sanctified the varna hierarchy and graded punishment — ‘the lower the varna, the higher the punishment’ — which drew
sharp critique and exposed the tension between order and equality lying at its heart.
Q — Discuss Kautilya’s theory of statecraft — the Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti), Mandala Siddhanta, Shadgunya-niti and the four Upayas — and his analysis of corruption. (UPSC 2017/2007)
Take Kautilya’s toolkit in order — the parts of the state, the map of neighbours, the six policies and four devices — and end with his diagnosis of corruption.
is a manual of administration, and

(Withdraw the rod and you get Matsyanyaya, ‘big fish eats small fish’ — punishment is the price of order.)
— the seven limbs: Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda/Bala, Mitra.
(An organic body — the king is the ‘Nabhi’ or navel, ministers its eyes, the treasury its blood; ‘one wheel alone does not turn the chariot’.)

(Your neighbour is your enemy and his neighbour your friend; a state lying between two powers — as Nepal lies between India and China — is the Madhyama or buffer.)
— six policies (Sandhi, Vigraha, Asana, Yana, Samshraya, Dvaidhibhava) and Sama, Dama, Danda, Bheda.
(Persuade → buy off → punish → divide: escalate only when the cheaper device fails.)
— ‘inevitable yet not desirable’; he lists ‘forty ways of embezzlement’.
(‘As it is impossible not to taste honey on the tongue’, and ‘a fish moving in water cannot be detected drinking it’.)

(Saptanga prefigures the modern elements of statehood; Mandala prefigures alliance theory.)

and geopolitics. Its normative anchor is the maxim that ‘in the happiness of the subjects lies the happiness of the king’, but the means are hard-headed.
— the science of the rod — is for Kautilya the decisive branch of knowledge, because coercive authority alone prevents
, the condition in which ‘the big fish eats the small fish’. Punishment wrongly used terrifies, left unused invites anarchy; used justly it upholds dharma, artha and kama alike.
The state is presented as an organism of

(the king, the ‘Nabhi’ or navel around which all else turns),

(the ally). No limb is dispensable and none suffices alone: ‘one wheel alone does not turn the chariot’. This organic conception strikingly anticipates the modern enumeration of the elements of statehood.
Foreign policy is mapped as a

or buffer — the position Nepal occupies between India and China — while a state outside the system altogether is the
or neutral. Enmity is therefore structural, a function of geography rather than sentiment, which is why the theory is read as an early doctrine of the
Within the mandala the vijigishu chooses among six measures —

: Sandhi (a peace treaty), Vigraha (hostility), Asana (keeping quiet or neutrality), Yana (marching to war), Samshraya (seeking shelter with a stronger king) and Dvaidhibhava (the double policy of peace with one and war with another). To achieve any of these he applies the four
(sowing division) — escalating only when the cheaper instrument has failed.

Kautilya thought corruption ‘inevitable yet not desirable’, and his realism about it is unmatched in ancient literature: ‘just as it is impossible not to taste honey on the tongue, so it is impossible for one dealing with government funds not to taste the king’s wealth’, and ‘a fish moving in water cannot be detected drinking it’. He catalogues

and prescribes institutional rather than merely moral remedies — frequent transfers of officials, protection and reward for informers and whistle-blowers, rewards for the honest, and punishment of ‘the entire chain’ rather than of the lowest offender alone.

Kautilya’s statecraft is remarkably systematic and practical — an ancient science of realpolitik, administration and geopolitics. Saptanga anticipates the organic theory of the state and the modern elements of statehood; the Mandala anticipates alliance theory and the
; and his treatment of corruption reads like a modern manual of administrative vigilance.
Q — Draw parallels and contrasts between Kautilya’s Arthashastra and the realist tradition of Machiavelli, and compare Dharmashastra and Arthashastra with reference to state power. (UPSC 2012/2010)
A two-part comparison — first Kautilya against Machiavelli, then Dharmashastra against Arthashastra on where power stands relative to morality.
: it is more accurate to call Machiavelli the ‘Italian Kautilya’ than Kautilya the ‘Indian Machiavelli’, as Nehru did.)
writing for a fragmented motherland, permitting ‘all sorts of means’ and an expansionist policy.
(Kautilya’s Bheda and Machiavelli’s advice to keep rivals disunited are the same device under two names.)
: ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli — Machiavelli’s Prince is harmless compared to Kautilya’s vijigishu’.
(The spies, poisoners and courtesan-agents of the Arthashastra have no parallel in The Prince.)
— ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains
(Power is a means for Kautilya, an end for Machiavelli — and ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’.)
(Manu’s king punishes to uphold the cosmic order; Kautilya’s punishes to keep the state strong, since artha is ‘supreme’ and dharma, kama and moksha depend on it.)
, a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics.
(Power is ruthless in operation yet answerable to a higher moral order.)
Nehru called Kautilya the ‘Indian Machiavelli’ and the label has stuck; but since the

rightly notes that it would be more accurate to call Machiavelli the ‘Italian Kautilya’. The comparison must therefore run forward from Kautilya, not backward, and any suggestion of influence is chronologically impossible.

of the first rank, writing amid political fragmentation for a motherland under threat — Kautilya for a Magadha facing invasion, Machiavelli for a divided Italy — and both make consolidation the supreme object. Both permit the ruler ‘all sorts of means’, both endorse an imperialist or expansionist foreign policy, and both in effect hold that the end justifies the means. Kautilya’s
— dividing the adversary — and Machiavelli’s counsel to keep rivals disunited are the same instrument under two different names.
judged that ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli — Machiavelli’s Prince is harmless compared to Kautilya’s vijigishu’. The judgment is defensible on detail: the
prescribes an elaborate machinery of spies, informers, poisoners and courtesan-agents, and a whole calculus of subversion, for which
offers no equivalent. Kautilya is thus the more thorough realist precisely because he is the more administrative one.
The difference lies in ethics: ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains
’. Kautilya’s king is enjoined to be ‘generous and kind’, is bound by the welfare of his subjects, and treats power as a

; Machiavelli’s prince rules ‘with an iron hand’ and treats power as self-justifying. Machiavelli offers generic counsel, Kautilya precise administrative detail — and, as the contrast is often put, ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’.
On state power the two Indian traditions differ in emphasis rather than in kind. The
: coercion exists to uphold the moral and cosmic order, and the king, bound by Raj Dharma, punishes in order to preserve varnashrama. The
and dharma peripheral: the king punishes to keep the state strong, because material well-being (‘artha’) is ‘supreme’, for ‘on it depend dharma, kama and moksha’.
Kautilya is a realist like Machiavelli but a

represents a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics: power is real, calculating and ruthless in operation, yet ultimately answerable to a higher moral order which the ruler did not create and cannot repeal.
Q — Examine the salient features of Buddhist political thought, assess whether it gave a greater ethical foundation to ancient Indian thought, and compare it with the Hindu tradition. (UPSC 2021)
Set out what is distinctive about Buddhist politics, then decide whether it is ethically superior to the Brahmanical tradition it broke from.
: Buddhism is ‘the rebel child of Hinduism’, egalitarian, rationalist and republican.
(The ‘Protestantism of the East’ — it bypassed the priest and the Sanskrit text, preaching in Pali to every varna.)
of men, not from a divine scheme.
(Once greed and theft appeared in an innocent society, men had to invent authority to restrain themselves.)
by consensus, ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’.
(‘The Great Elect’ — the people choose one man and pay him a share of the grain to keep order: a social contract centuries before Hobbes and Locke.)
— government by ethical persuasion, not danda; the
(Ashoka conquers hearts rather than land, and pointedly never made Buddhism a state religion — an implicit secularism.)
praises its commitment to public discussion.
— republican vs monarchical, elected king vs divine personality, Dhamma vs Danda, and
(This-worldly and deliberative against other-worldly and hierarchical.)
(Which is exactly why Ambedkar chose Buddhism in 1956 as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism.)
calls Buddhism ‘the rebel child of Hinduism’ — an

tradition, the ‘Protestantism of the East’, which challenged caste, dispensed with the priestly intermediary and Vedic ritual, and preached in Pali rather than Sanskrit so that the message reached every varna.
accordingly treats the Buddha as a genuine political philosopher and not merely a religious teacher.
Where the Hindu tradition derives kingship from the need to end
ordained in the cosmic scheme, the Buddhist account is historical and moral: the state arises from the

of men. In an originally innocent society the growth of greed, property and theft made restraint necessary, and men themselves devised authority to supply it. Political power is therefore a human remedy for a human failing, not a divine institution.
It follows that the king is

— ‘the Great Elect’ — chosen by the people to keep order in return for a share of their produce, and remaining ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’. Authority is thus conditional upon consent and upon performance of the agreed function, giving Buddhism a theory of
decentralised democracy, equality and the social contract
many centuries before Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau — reflected institutionally in the ganasangha republics and in the deliberative procedure of the sangha itself.
— ethical persuasion — rather than by danda: the ideal ruler is the

who ‘wins others by the Dhamma Chakra’, conquering hearts instead of territory. Ashoka’s polity after Kalinga embodied this, yet he ‘never made Buddhism a state religion’ and enjoined respect for all sects — an implicit secularism.
praises the tradition’s ‘foundational commitment to public communication and discussion’, tracing India’s argumentative and deliberative ethos to the Buddhist councils.
The contrast is systematic: this-worldly against other-worldly;

; a king elected by the MahaSammat against a king of ‘divine personality’; the Chakravartin winning hearts against the vijigishu acquiring land; Dhamma and Panchsheel against Danda and Mandala; and, most consequentially, the
rejection of caste in favour of equality
against the Brahmanical hierarchy of varna. Where the Hindu tradition legitimises order through birth, the Buddhist legitimises it through consent and conduct.
Buddhist thought did lend a greater
foundation to ancient Indian political thought — egalitarian, rational and consent-based — anticipating ideas the West reached only much later. That is precisely why
chose it in 1956 as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism, converting at Nagpur with lakhs of followers.
Q — Assess Sir Syed Ahmed Khan as a social reformer and modernizer, tracing his transition from champion of Hindu-Muslim unity to originator of the two-nation theory. (UPSC 2021/2013)
Two halves — credit him as a reformer, then explain why the preacher of unity turned into the father of the two-nation theory.
— Muslim upliftment is ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith ‘most compatible with science and rationality’.
(‘The Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’.)
(MAO College grew into Aligarh Muslim University; his standing among Muslims is compared to Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s among Hindus.)
— a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance.
(He denounced purdah, polygamy and easy divorce as social evils rather than sanctified custom.)
— a common Indian nationhood; by ‘qaum’ he meant both communities.
(‘Hindus and Muslims are the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — sharing ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’.)
— fearing that under elections the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, he opposed representative government and the Congress.
(Counting heads where the majority is permanent means permanent minority subordination — hence the ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’.)
— his educational and political legacies pull in opposite directions.
(AMU on one side, the ideological seed of Partition on the other.)

held that Muslim upliftment was ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith he regarded as ‘most compatible with science and rationality’. Writing after 1857, when the community had turned inward and boycotted English education, his central message was the reconciliation of revelation with reason: ‘the Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’. Faith and modern knowledge, he insisted, cannot contradict each other because both proceed from the same source.
He acted on this creed institutionally. He launched the journal
to reform Muslim manners and opinion, founded a scientific society to translate Western works into Urdu, and established the
and became the seedbed of a modern Muslim professional class. His status among Muslims is fairly compared to
He was, in the textbook’s phrase, a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance and irrational custom wherever he found them. He denounced
as social evils rather than sanctified practice, and urged that scripture be interpreted in the light of reason and changing circumstance — a position that drew the hostility of the orthodox ulema.

In his earlier phase he was an unambiguous exponent of a common Indian nationhood. Hindus and Muslims are ‘the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — injure one and the bride is disfigured — for they share ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’. By
(nation) he expressly meant ‘both Hindus and Muslims’, and he worked closely with Hindu leaders in educational and civic causes.
The shift came with the prospect of

. Sir Syed feared that where elections turn on counting heads in a society of permanent majorities and minorities, the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, reducing Muslims to permanent subordination. He therefore turned against parliamentary self-government, opposed the Congress, and sought an ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’, becoming the originator of the

— the doctrine that Hindus and Muslims form two distinct nations. The Urdu-Hindi controversy, his dependence on government funding for the Aligarh college, and rising Hindu revivalism all accelerated the transition.

Sir Syed was a genuine modernizer who dragged a defeated and conservative community toward science, English education and social reform. But his later communal politics laid the ideological seed of Partition, so that his educational legacy at Aligarh and his political legacy in the two-nation theory pull in exactly opposite directions.
Q — Analyse Sri Aurobindo’s theory of cultural/spiritual nationalism, his conception of Swaraj and his idea of freedom. (UPSC 2017/2016/2014/2013)
Three linked ideas — the nation as spirit, Swaraj as complete independence, and freedom as inner self-realisation.
saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’.
(Nationalism is not a political programme but a way of life like religion — the patriot is a devotee, not a party worker.)
— ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the
nation is a faith, a religion, the nation has a spirit
(Herder’s national spirit + Bankim’s Mother India as Goddess + Vivekananda’s Neo-Vedanta — India’s ‘divine mission’ is to give spirituality to the world.)
— in his extremist phase he rejected Moderate constitutionalism and theorised organised resistance.
(Swadeshi, boycott and non-cooperation — the doctrinal ground on which Gandhi’s Satyagraha was later built.)
— the first to read Swaraj as
(‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’; to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’.)
— the liberal view is ‘mechanical’ and the socialist neglects the individual; true freedom is
(‘Obeying the law of our own existence’ — swadharma — so a man free of foreign rule but enslaved to his appetites is not free.)
— he raised nationalism from programme to vocation, though critics call it reactionary and idealistic.
(By rooting it in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma he radicalised the freedom movement.)

saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’. For him nationalism was not a mere political programme but a way of life like religion: the patriot approaches the nation as a devotee approaches the divine, with faith and self-surrender rather than a calculation of interest. This converted the freedom struggle from a constitutional claim into a spiritual vocation.
claim that ‘the nation is natural and has a spirit’ — and drawing on
Neo-Vedanta, Aurobindo held that ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the
nation is a faith, the nation is a religion, the nation has a spirit
’. India is not a territory but a living Mother with a
— to give spirituality to a materialist world — so her subjection is a spiritual and not merely a political wrong.
In his extremist phase Aurobindo dismissed the Moderates’ constitutional petitioning as futile and pioneered a systematic theory of

— organised non-cooperation with an alien administration, backed by swadeshi, boycott and national education, to be abandoned only if repression made resistance impossible. This body of doctrine prepared the ground on which
Satyagraha would be built a decade later.
He was the first Indian leader to interpret Swaraj as

— complete independence rather than colonial self-government within the Empire — to be won through swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance. ‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’, he wrote, and to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’. Swaraj is thus the ‘necessary condition for India to accomplish its destined goal’ — the political shell within which the spiritual mission can be realised.

Aurobindo found the liberal, near-anarchic conception of liberty ‘mechanical’ — an absence of external restraint that says nothing about what the free man becomes — and the socialist conception neglectful of the individual. Real freedom is
: ‘obeying the law of our own existence’, that is, swadharma. A man released from foreign rule but enslaved to his own appetites has not become free. His later thought —
Sacchidananda, the Supermind and Integral Yoga
— accordingly makes national self-realisation one stage in the spiritual evolution of humanity as a whole.

Aurobindo raised nationalism from a political programme to a spiritual vocation. Critics call his spiritual nationalism reactionary, idealistic and open to majoritarian appropriation; yet by rooting freedom in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma rather than a narrow creed, and by demanding Purna Swaraj when others asked only for reform, he decisively radicalised the Indian freedom movement.

Q — Evaluate Ambedkar’s idea of social justice — annihilation of caste, critique of Hinduism and of Marxism, and his conception of social/economic/political democracy — comparing his egalitarian justice with Rawls. (UPSC 2022/2020/2018/2016/2013)
Build Ambedkar’s theory of justice upward from caste, then measure it against Rawls’ procedural justice.
— caste is ‘not the division of labour but the
(A guild you may leave; a caste you are born into and must marry within — so inter-caste marriage, not ritual reform, is the real solvent.)
— ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, sanctified by the Vedas and the Manusmriti.
(He would ‘put dynamite’ on the Manusmriti, and finding reform impossible from within, converted to Buddhism in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’.)
— democracy is ‘a way of life’ on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’; political democracy must be completed by
(One man one vote is worthless if the same man may not draw water from the village well.)
(Not merely obeying the text but internalising its spirit — self-restraint, due process, respect for dissent — in a soil he called ‘essentially undemocratic’.)
— religion is not mere ‘opium’, and ‘society is more exploitative than the state’.
(Buddhism, built on karuna, samata and prajna, liberates; and the untouchable is humiliated by his neighbours, so the state must be his instrument of emancipation, not his enemy.)
(Rawls reasons from a hypothetical veil of ignorance; Ambedkar starts from a real history of humiliation and demands safeguards to undo it.)
— ‘chief architect of the Constitution’ and himself born a Mahar — made the
he argues that caste is ‘not the division of labour but the
’: a guild divides work and may be left, whereas caste divides human beings themselves into fixed, graded compartments one is born into. Its steel frame is
, which is why he held that inter-caste marriage and inter-dining, not the reform of ritual, are the real solvents of the system.
Caste for Ambedkar is not an excrescence but the essence: ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, a graded inequality sanctified by the Vedas and above all by the

, on which he said he would ‘put dynamite’ and which he publicly burnt in 1927. Because the sanction is scriptural, reform from within is impossible — destroy belief in the sanctity of the shastras and caste collapses. Finding no such reform forthcoming, he
in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’.

For Ambedkar democracy is not a form of government but ‘a way of life’, resting on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’, which he traced to the Buddha rather than to the French Revolution. Hence his warning that India was entering a life of contradictions: political equality of one man one vote alongside social and economic inequality. Political democracy must therefore be completed by
, for ‘political democracy cannot last unless there lies at its base social democracy’ — the vote is empty if the voter may not draw water from the village well.

Borrowing the phrase from Grote, Ambedkar meant not mere obedience to the constitutional text but internalisation of its spirit — self-restraint by those in power, respect for forms and for dissent, and the settling of conflict by due process rather than agitation — a habit he thought had to be deliberately cultivated because Indian soil was ‘essentially undemocratic’. Alongside it he urged state ownership of key industries and of land, so that concentrated economic power could not defeat formal equality.

Ambedkar rejected two Marxist claims. First, that religion is mere ‘opium’: Buddhism, resting on karuna, samata and prajna, is a liberating morality and not a narcotic. Second, that the state is the chief instrument of oppression — for Ambedkar ‘society is more exploitative than the state’, since the untouchable is humiliated by his own neighbours and not primarily by officials, so the state must be strengthened as an instrument of emancipation. He also rejected violent revolution and the dictatorship of the proletariat in favour of constitutional methods.

contentText: Syllabus — Indian Political Thought: Dharmashastra, Arthashastra and Buddhist traditions; Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar, M.N. Roy. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 9) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the ancient traditions — Dharmashastra (Manu), Arthashastra (Kautilya) and Buddhist political thought — and the modern thinkers Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, Sri Aurobindo, M.K. Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar and M.N. Roy. Must-know thinkers & concepts:  Manu (dharma, varna), Kautilya (Saptanga, Mandala, Danda-niti, Matsyanyaya), Buddha (MahaSammat, Dhamma), Sir Syed (two-nation theory), Aurobindo (spiritual nationalism, Purna Swaraj), Gandhi (Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya, Trusteeship), Ambedkar (annihilation of caste, social democracy), M.N. Roy (radical humanism). PYQ trend:  Gandhi (2020/2019/2016/2015) and Ambedkar (2022/2020/2018/2016/2013) are the highest-yield; also Kautilya’s statecraft (2017/2012/2010/2007), Buddhist ethics (2021), Aurobindo (2017/2016/2014/2013), Sir Syed (2021/2013), Dharma (2020), M.N. Roy. Master Questions Q — Explicate the ideological components of Gandhism — Truth/Ahimsa, Satyagraha, Swaraj, Sarvodaya and Trusteeship — and evaluate his critique of modern Western civilization and his view of the state. (UPSC 2020/2019/2016/2015) What it’s asking:  List the building blocks of Gandhi’s thought one by one, then judge his attack on modern civilization and on the state itself. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Truth & Ahimsa  — the twin foundation: ‘God and truth are inseparable’ and non-violence is ‘not the resort of the weak but the power of the strong’.  (Ahimsa is active love, not cowardly submission — the man who runs away from the blow is not practising it.) 2. Satyagraha  — satya + agraha = ‘soul-force over brute-force through self-suffering’, aimed ‘against the evil, not the evil-doer’.  (The satyagrahi breaks the unjust law openly, accepts the lathi-blow and the jail term without retaliating, so the opponent’s conscience — not his body — is defeated.)   Martin Luther King : ‘Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi furnished the method’. 3. Swaraj & Ram Rajya  — liberty as  self-rule plus self-control , political, economic, social and cultural.  (Not swapping a white ruler for a brown one: it is the village governing itself and the individual mastering his own appetites — ending in Ram Rajya, a near-stateless order of self-governing ‘oceanic circles’.) 4. Sarvodaya & Trusteeship  — from Ruskin’s  Unto This Last , ‘the uplift of all’ through bread labour, with the rich as ‘trustees, not owners’.  (The mill-owner keeps the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers, drawing only what he needs — ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’.) 5. Critique of modernity & the state  — in  Hind Swaraj  modern Western civilization is ‘satanic’ and materialist, and the state is ‘a soulless machine’ resting on coercion.  (Railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than civilisation.) 6. Conclusion  — ends and means are continuous: ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’.  (A freedom won by terror would itself have been an unfree India.) Model Answer 1. Truth & Ahimsa.  Gandhi denied there was any ‘Gandhism’;  Humayun Kabir  called him ‘not a philosopher but a strategist… a psychologist’, and his ideas — set out in  Hind Swaraj  and  My Experiments with Truth , drawing on the Gita, Tolstoy and Ruskin — rest on two inseparable foundations. ‘God and truth are inseparable’, and  Ahimsa  is the only means of realising truth: it is ‘not the resort of the weak but the power of the strong’, active love rather than the cowardice of the man who simply runs away from the blow. 2. Satyagraha.  From truth and non-violence flows  Satyagraha  (satya + agraha) — ‘soul-force over brute-force through self-suffering’, directed ‘against the evil, not the evil-doer’, and therefore quite distinct from mere passive resistance, which is the weapon of the weak. In practice the satyagrahi disobeys the unjust law openly, invites arrest and absorbs the blow without returning it, converting the opponent by melting his conscience instead of crushing his body.  Martin Luther King  acknowledged the debt: ‘Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi furnished the method’. 3. Swaraj & Ram Rajya.  Gandhi’s idea of liberty is  self-rule and self-control  together — political, economic, social and cultural. Merely replacing English rulers by Indian ones would be English rule without the Englishman; genuine Swaraj means the village governing its own affairs through Panchayati Raj and the individual governing his own appetites. Its culmination is  Ram Rajya , a stateless society of ‘oceanic circles’ in which the individual is the centre and no circle dominates another. His famous image guards this from parochialism: ‘I do not want my house to be walled in… I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house… but I refuse to be blown off my feet’. 4. Sarvodaya & Trusteeship.  From Ruskin’s  Unto This Last  Gandhi drew  Sarvodaya  — ‘the uplift of all’ rather than the greatest good of the greatest number — resting on  bread labour  and on  Trusteeship . Capitalists are ‘trustees, not owners’: the mill-owner retains the mill but holds its wealth in trust for his workers and for society, drawing only what he genuinely needs, since ‘there is enough for need but not for greed’. This substitutes class cooperation and a change of heart for the Marxist expropriation of the propertied class. 5. Critique of modernity & the state.  In  Hind Swaraj  Gandhi condemns modern Western civilization as materialist and ‘satanic’ — it multiplies wants instead of mastering them, and its railways, lawyers and doctors spread disease, litigation and dependence rather than true civilisation, which he defines as that mode of conduct which points out to man the path of duty. The  state  is condemned on the same ground: it is ‘a soulless machine’ based on coercion, representing violence in a concentrated and organised form, and it stunts the self-reliance and moral growth of the individual. His ideal is therefore ‘enlightened anarchy’ — government reduced to the minimum as men learn to govern themselves. 6. Conclusion.  Gandhism fuses ethics and politics through the ‘continuity of ends and means’ — ‘if we take care of the means, the end will take care of itself’, for a freedom won by terror would itself be unfree. Though Trusteeship and Ram Rajya are criticised as impractical and utopian, Gandhi’s non-violent Satyagraha remains his enduring contribution to world politics. Q — Explain the sources and salient features of ancient Indian political thought, and examine the significance of Dharma in the Dharmashastra (Manu) tradition. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  Where ancient Indian thought comes from, what marks it out, and why Dharma is its master-concept. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Sources & riti  — thought derives from  riti , the cosmic order known through spiritual experience, and from the shrutis and smritis (the  Manusmriti ).  (Riti does for India what natural law does for the West — a higher order the ruler did not make and cannot unmake.) 2. Salient features  — ‘enormous continuity’,  communitarian, pluralistic and cosmopolitan , but non-critical and regressive about history.  (Sant Tukaram: ‘the entire world is a family’ — the individual sits inside kula, jati and society, never against them.) 3. Dharma & Danda in continuum  — ‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’, differing in degree, not in kind.  (Politics is a chapter of ethics here, not the separate autonomous science it becomes in Machiavelli.) 4. Manu & the significance of Dharma  —  Manu , the ‘first law-giver’: ‘ Prithvim Dharma Dhritam ’, dharma is that which holds life on earth.  (It is social cement — each varna and ashrama performing its own svadharma keeps the whole edifice standing.) 5. Matsyanyaya & the king under law  — dharma’s absence brings  arajakta  and  Matsya Nyaya .  (‘The big fish eats the small fish’ — anarchy, where strength alone decides.)  Hence the king has ‘divine personality’ but  no divine rights . 6. Conclusion  — dharma both legitimises and limits kingship, yet sanctifies varna hierarchy —  Ambedkar’s  target.  (‘The lower the varna, the higher the punishment’.) Model Answer 1. Sources & riti.  Ancient Indian (‘Hindu’) political thought derives from  riti  — the all-pervading cosmic order, discoverable through spiritual experience, which orders nature and society alike. It performs the same office as the Western concept of  natural law : a standard the ruler neither creates nor can abolish, and against which his commands are measured. Its textual sources are the  Vedic corpus  — the shrutis (the Vedas, ‘that which is heard’) and the smritis (‘that which is remembered’), above all the  Manusmriti . 2. Salient features.  Four features stand out. It shows ‘enormous continuity’ of dharma and danda across centuries rather than sharp ruptures. It is  communitarian  — the individual is always located within family, kula, jati and society, never posed against them as in Western individualism. It is  pluralistic and cosmopolitan ;  Sant Tukaram’s  ‘the entire world is a family’ captures the vasudhaiva kutumbakam spirit. But it is also  non-critical , taking a regressive rather than a progressive view of history — the golden age lies behind, in Satya Yuga, and the present is a fall from it. 3. Dharma & Danda in continuum.  ‘Dharma Shastras are books on law; Danda Shastras are books on politics’ — but they differ only in  degree , for Indian thought treats them not ‘in silos but in a continuum’. Politics is thus a chapter of ethics rather than an autonomous science, unlike the Machiavellian separation of the two. Within the  Dharmashastra  tradition dharma is the core and danda the periphery; in the Arthashastra the emphasis is exactly reversed. 4. Manu & the significance of Dharma.  Manu , the ‘first law-giver’ and Manasputra of Brahma, is the chief exponent of this tradition.  Dharma  — at once moral, natural and social order — is its master concept: ‘ Prithvim Dharma Dhritam ’, dharma is that which holds life on earth. It works as social cement, each varna and each ashrama discharging its own svadharma so that the whole edifice stands; and it is also the source of the king’s obligations, since Raj Dharma binds him as tightly as it binds the subject. 5. Matsyanyaya & the king under law.  The significance of dharma is shown negatively by what follows its absence:  arajakta  (anarchy) and  Matsya Nyaya  — literally the law of the fish, where ‘the big fish eats the small fish’ and strength alone decides, the Indian equivalent of the Hobbesian state of nature. Kingship exists precisely to prevent this. Yet although the king possesses a ‘divine personality’, he has  no divine rights  of the European kind: he is bound by Raj Dharma and stands  under the law , and a king who violates dharma forfeits his claim to obedience. 6. Conclusion.  Dharma is therefore the master concept of the ancient Indian polity — it simultaneously legitimises kingship and limits it, anticipating constitutionalism without a constitution. Yet the same tradition sanctified the varna hierarchy and graded punishment — ‘the lower the varna, the higher the punishment’ — which drew  Ambedkar’s  sharp critique and exposed the tension between order and equality lying at its heart. Q — Discuss Kautilya’s theory of statecraft — the Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti), Mandala Siddhanta, Shadgunya-niti and the four Upayas — and his analysis of corruption. (UPSC 2017/2007) What it’s asking:  Take Kautilya’s toolkit in order — the parts of the state, the map of neighbours, the six policies and four devices — and end with his diagnosis of corruption. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The text & Danda-niti  — the  Arthashastra  is a manual of administration, and  danda-niti , the science of the rod, is what holds society together.  (Withdraw the rod and you get Matsyanyaya, ‘big fish eats small fish’ — punishment is the price of order.) 2. Saptanga  — the seven limbs: Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda/Bala, Mitra.  (An organic body — the king is the ‘Nabhi’ or navel, ministers its eyes, the treasury its blood; ‘one wheel alone does not turn the chariot’.) 3. Mandala Siddhanta  — concentric rings of natural enemy (Ari) and natural friend (Mitra) around the  vijigishu .  (Your neighbour is your enemy and his neighbour your friend; a state lying between two powers — as Nepal lies between India and China — is the Madhyama or buffer.) 4. Shadgunya-niti & four Upayas  — six policies (Sandhi, Vigraha, Asana, Yana, Samshraya, Dvaidhibhava) and Sama, Dama, Danda, Bheda.  (Persuade → buy off → punish → divide: escalate only when the cheaper device fails.) 5. Corruption  — ‘inevitable yet not desirable’; he lists ‘forty ways of embezzlement’.  (‘As it is impossible not to taste honey on the tongue’, and ‘a fish moving in water cannot be detected drinking it’.)  Remedies: transfers, whistle-blowers, rewards. 6. Conclusion  — an ancient science of realpolitik anticipating the organic theory of the state and the  balance of power .  (Saptanga prefigures the modern elements of statehood; Mandala prefigures alliance theory.) Model Answer 1. The text & Danda-niti.  Kautilya’s   Arthashastra  is essentially ‘a book on the art of administration’ and the first Indian text of  statecraft  and geopolitics. Its normative anchor is the maxim that ‘in the happiness of the subjects lies the happiness of the king’, but the means are hard-headed.  Danda-niti  — the science of the rod — is for Kautilya the decisive branch of knowledge, because coercive authority alone prevents  Matsyanyaya , the condition in which ‘the big fish eats the small fish’. Punishment wrongly used terrifies, left unused invites anarchy; used justly it upholds dharma, artha and kama alike. 2. Saptanga (Sapta Prakriti).  The state is presented as an organism of  seven limbs , exactly as a body has limbs:  Swami  (the king, the ‘Nabhi’ or navel around which all else turns),  Amatya  (ministers, its eyes and ears),  Janapada  (territory with its population),  Durga  (the fort),  Kosha  (the treasury — ‘all undertakings depend upon Kosha’, its blood),  Danda or Bala  (the army, its arms) and  Mitra  (the ally). No limb is dispensable and none suffices alone: ‘one wheel alone does not turn the chariot’. This organic conception strikingly anticipates the modern enumeration of the elements of statehood. 3. Mandala Siddhanta.  Foreign policy is mapped as a  mandala  — concentric circles drawn around the  vijigishu , ‘the one who aspires to victory’. The immediate neighbour is the natural enemy ( Ari ), the neighbour beyond him the natural friend ( Mitra ), and so outward in alternating rings; a strong state situated between two rivals is the  Madhyama  or buffer — the position Nepal occupies between India and China — while a state outside the system altogether is the  Udasina  or neutral. Enmity is therefore structural, a function of geography rather than sentiment, which is why the theory is read as an early doctrine of the  balance of power . 4. Shadgunya-niti & the four Upayas.  Within the mandala the vijigishu chooses among six measures —  Shadgunya-niti : Sandhi (a peace treaty), Vigraha (hostility), Asana (keeping quiet or neutrality), Yana (marching to war), Samshraya (seeking shelter with a stronger king) and Dvaidhibhava (the double policy of peace with one and war with another). To achieve any of these he applies the four  Upayas  in ascending order of cost:  Sama  (conciliation),  Dama  (gifts or bribery),  Danda  (force) and  Bheda  (sowing division) — escalating only when the cheaper instrument has failed. 5. Corruption.  Kautilya thought corruption ‘inevitable yet not desirable’, and his realism about it is unmatched in ancient literature: ‘just as it is impossible not to taste honey on the tongue, so it is impossible for one dealing with government funds not to taste the king’s wealth’, and ‘a fish moving in water cannot be detected drinking it’. He catalogues  forty ways of embezzlement  and prescribes institutional rather than merely moral remedies — frequent transfers of officials, protection and reward for informers and whistle-blowers, rewards for the honest, and punishment of ‘the entire chain’ rather than of the lowest offender alone. 6. Conclusion.  Kautilya’s statecraft is remarkably systematic and practical — an ancient science of realpolitik, administration and geopolitics. Saptanga anticipates the organic theory of the state and the modern elements of statehood; the Mandala anticipates alliance theory and the  balance of power ; and his treatment of corruption reads like a modern manual of administrative vigilance. Q — Draw parallels and contrasts between Kautilya’s Arthashastra and the realist tradition of Machiavelli, and compare Dharmashastra and Arthashastra with reference to state power. (UPSC 2012/2010) What it’s asking:  A two-part comparison — first Kautilya against Machiavelli, then Dharmashastra against Arthashastra on where power stands relative to morality. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Chronology first  — the  Arthashastra  precedes  The Prince  by about  1800 years .  ( Upinder Singh : it is more accurate to call Machiavelli the ‘Italian Kautilya’ than Kautilya the ‘Indian Machiavelli’, as Nehru did.) 2. Parallels  — both are  realists  writing for a fragmented motherland, permitting ‘all sorts of means’ and an expansionist policy.  (Kautilya’s Bheda and Machiavelli’s advice to keep rivals disunited are the same device under two names.) 3. Weber’s verdict  —  Max Weber : ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli — Machiavelli’s Prince is harmless compared to Kautilya’s vijigishu’.  (The spies, poisoners and courtesan-agents of the Arthashastra have no parallel in The Prince.) 4. The decisive contrast  — ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains  under dharma ’.  (Power is a means for Kautilya, an end for Machiavelli — and ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’.) 5. Dharmashastra vs Arthashastra  — Manu subordinates  danda to dharma ; Kautilya makes  danda central .  (Manu’s king punishes to uphold the cosmic order; Kautilya’s punishes to keep the state strong, since artha is ‘supreme’ and dharma, kama and moksha depend on it.) 6. Conclusion  — Kautilya is a  dharma-bounded realist , a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics.  (Power is ruthless in operation yet answerable to a higher moral order.) Model Answer 1. Chronology first.  Nehru called Kautilya the ‘Indian Machiavelli’ and the label has stuck; but since the  Arthashastra  predates  The Prince  by roughly  1800 years ,  Upinder Singh  rightly notes that it would be more accurate to call Machiavelli the ‘Italian Kautilya’. The comparison must therefore run forward from Kautilya, not backward, and any suggestion of influence is chronologically impossible. 2. Parallels.  Both are  realists  of the first rank, writing amid political fragmentation for a motherland under threat — Kautilya for a Magadha facing invasion, Machiavelli for a divided Italy — and both make consolidation the supreme object. Both permit the ruler ‘all sorts of means’, both endorse an imperialist or expansionist foreign policy, and both in effect hold that the end justifies the means. Kautilya’s  Bheda  — dividing the adversary — and Machiavelli’s counsel to keep rivals disunited are the same instrument under two different names. 3. Weber’s verdict.  Max Weber  judged that ‘Kautilya is more Machiavelli than Machiavelli — Machiavelli’s Prince is harmless compared to Kautilya’s vijigishu’. The judgment is defensible on detail: the  Arthashastra  prescribes an elaborate machinery of spies, informers, poisoners and courtesan-agents, and a whole calculus of subversion, for which  The Prince  offers no equivalent. Kautilya is thus the more thorough realist precisely because he is the more administrative one. 4. The decisive contrast.  The difference lies in ethics: ‘for Machiavelli the Prince is above religion; for Kautilya the king remains  under dharma ’. Kautilya’s king is enjoined to be ‘generous and kind’, is bound by the welfare of his subjects, and treats power as a  means, not an end ; Machiavelli’s prince rules ‘with an iron hand’ and treats power as self-justifying. Machiavelli offers generic counsel, Kautilya precise administrative detail — and, as the contrast is often put, ‘Kautilya got his king, Machiavelli never got his prince’. 5. Dharmashastra vs Arthashastra.  On state power the two Indian traditions differ in emphasis rather than in kind. The  Dharmashastra  of  Manu  subordinates  danda to dharma : coercion exists to uphold the moral and cosmic order, and the king, bound by Raj Dharma, punishes in order to preserve varnashrama. The  Arthashastra  of  Kautilya  makes  danda central  and dharma peripheral: the king punishes to keep the state strong, because material well-being (‘artha’) is ‘supreme’, for ‘on it depend dharma, kama and moksha’. 6. Conclusion.  Kautilya is a realist like Machiavelli but a  dharma-bounded  one, which is why the  Arthashastra  represents a distinctively Indian synthesis of statecraft and ethics: power is real, calculating and ruthless in operation, yet ultimately answerable to a higher moral order which the ruler did not create and cannot repeal. Q — Examine the salient features of Buddhist political thought, assess whether it gave a greater ethical foundation to ancient Indian thought, and compare it with the Hindu tradition. (UPSC 2021) What it’s asking:  Set out what is distinctive about Buddhist politics, then decide whether it is ethically superior to the Brahmanical tradition it broke from. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The rebel child  —  Bhikhu Parekh : Buddhism is ‘the rebel child of Hinduism’, egalitarian, rationalist and republican.  (The ‘Protestantism of the East’ — it bypassed the priest and the Sanskrit text, preaching in Pali to every varna.) 2. Origin of the state  — the state arises from the  moral fall  of men, not from a divine scheme.  (Once greed and theft appeared in an innocent society, men had to invent authority to restrain themselves.) 3. MahaSammat  — the king is  elected  by consensus, ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’.  (‘The Great Elect’ — the people choose one man and pay him a share of the grain to keep order: a social contract centuries before Hobbes and Locke.) 4. Rule by Dhamma  — government by ethical persuasion, not danda; the  Chakravartin  ‘wins others by the Dhamma Chakra’.  (Ashoka conquers hearts rather than land, and pointedly never made Buddhism a state religion — an implicit secularism.)   Amartya Sen  praises its commitment to public discussion. 5. Buddhist vs Hindu  — republican vs monarchical, elected king vs divine personality, Dhamma vs Danda, and  rejection of caste  vs Brahmanical hierarchy.  (This-worldly and deliberative against other-worldly and hierarchical.) 6. Conclusion  — a genuinely stronger  ethical and deliberative  foundation.  (Which is exactly why Ambedkar chose Buddhism in 1956 as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism.) Model Answer 1. The rebel child.  Bhikhu Parekh  calls Buddhism ‘the rebel child of Hinduism’ — an  egalitarian, rationalist and republican  tradition, the ‘Protestantism of the East’, which challenged caste, dispensed with the priestly intermediary and Vedic ritual, and preached in Pali rather than Sanskrit so that the message reached every varna.  Gail Omvedt  accordingly treats the Buddha as a genuine political philosopher and not merely a religious teacher. 2. Origin of the state.  Where the Hindu tradition derives kingship from the need to end  arajakta  ordained in the cosmic scheme, the Buddhist account is historical and moral: the state arises from the  moral fall or corruption  of men. In an originally innocent society the growth of greed, property and theft made restraint necessary, and men themselves devised authority to supply it. Political power is therefore a human remedy for a human failing, not a divine institution. 3. MahaSammat.  It follows that the king is  elected  by consensus in the  MahaSammat  — ‘the Great Elect’ — chosen by the people to keep order in return for a share of their produce, and remaining ‘only primus inter pares, by virtue of a social contract’. Authority is thus conditional upon consent and upon performance of the agreed function, giving Buddhism a theory of  decentralised democracy, equality and the social contract  many centuries before Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau — reflected institutionally in the ganasangha republics and in the deliberative procedure of the sangha itself. 4. Rule by Dhamma.  Government is by  Dhamma  — ethical persuasion — rather than by danda: the ideal ruler is the  Chakravartin  who ‘wins others by the Dhamma Chakra’, conquering hearts instead of territory. Ashoka’s polity after Kalinga embodied this, yet he ‘never made Buddhism a state religion’ and enjoined respect for all sects — an implicit secularism.  Amartya Sen  praises the tradition’s ‘foundational commitment to public communication and discussion’, tracing India’s argumentative and deliberative ethos to the Buddhist councils. 5. Buddhist vs Hindu.  The contrast is systematic: this-worldly against other-worldly;  republican against monarchical ; a king elected by the MahaSammat against a king of ‘divine personality’; the Chakravartin winning hearts against the vijigishu acquiring land; Dhamma and Panchsheel against Danda and Mandala; and, most consequentially, the  rejection of caste in favour of equality  against the Brahmanical hierarchy of varna. Where the Hindu tradition legitimises order through birth, the Buddhist legitimises it through consent and conduct. 6. Conclusion.  Buddhist thought did lend a greater  ethical and deliberative  foundation to ancient Indian political thought — egalitarian, rational and consent-based — anticipating ideas the West reached only much later. That is precisely why  Ambedkar  chose it in 1956 as the emancipatory alternative to caste Hinduism, converting at Nagpur with lakhs of followers. Q — Assess Sir Syed Ahmed Khan as a social reformer and modernizer, tracing his transition from champion of Hindu-Muslim unity to originator of the two-nation theory. (UPSC 2021/2013) What it’s asking:  Two halves — credit him as a reformer, then explain why the preacher of unity turned into the father of the two-nation theory. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Core creed  — Muslim upliftment is ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith ‘most compatible with science and rationality’.  (‘The Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’.) 2. Educational modernizer  — the journal  Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq , a scientific society and  MAO College .  (MAO College grew into Aligarh Muslim University; his standing among Muslims is compared to Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s among Hindus.) 3. Social reformer  — a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance.  (He denounced purdah, polygamy and easy divorce as social evils rather than sanctified custom.) 4. Phase 1 — Hindu-Muslim unity  — a common Indian nationhood; by ‘qaum’ he meant both communities.  (‘Hindus and Muslims are the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — sharing ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’.) 5. Phase 2 — the two-nation theory  — fearing that under elections the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, he opposed representative government and the Congress.  (Counting heads where the majority is permanent means permanent minority subordination — hence the ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’.) 6. Conclusion  — his educational and political legacies pull in opposite directions.  (AMU on one side, the ideological seed of Partition on the other.) Model Answer 1. Core creed.  Sir Syed Ahmed Khan  held that Muslim upliftment was ‘possible only with the modernization of Islam’, a faith he regarded as ‘most compatible with science and rationality’. Writing after 1857, when the community had turned inward and boycotted English education, his central message was the reconciliation of revelation with reason: ‘the Muslim youth should hold the book of science in one hand and the Quran in the other’. Faith and modern knowledge, he insisted, cannot contradict each other because both proceed from the same source. 2. Educational modernizer.  He acted on this creed institutionally. He launched the journal  Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq  to reform Muslim manners and opinion, founded a scientific society to translate Western works into Urdu, and established the  Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College  at Aligarh, which grew into  Aligarh Muslim University  and became the seedbed of a modern Muslim professional class. His status among Muslims is fairly compared to  Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s  among Hindus. 3. Social reformer.  He was, in the textbook’s phrase, a ‘champion of democratic ideals and freedom of speech’ who attacked religious intolerance and irrational custom wherever he found them. He denounced  purdah, polygamy and easy divorce  as social evils rather than sanctified practice, and urged that scripture be interpreted in the light of reason and changing circumstance — a position that drew the hostility of the orthodox ulema. 4. Phase 1 — Hindu-Muslim unity.  In his earlier phase he was an unambiguous exponent of a common Indian nationhood. Hindus and Muslims are ‘the two eyes of the beautiful bride, India’ — injure one and the bride is disfigured — for they share ‘the same soil… the same ruler… the hardships of a famine’. By  qaum  (nation) he expressly meant ‘both Hindus and Muslims’, and he worked closely with Hindu leaders in educational and civic causes. 5. Phase 2 — the two-nation theory.  The shift came with the prospect of  representative government . Sir Syed feared that where elections turn on counting heads in a society of permanent majorities and minorities, the Hindu majority would ‘totally override the interests of the smaller community’, reducing Muslims to permanent subordination. He therefore turned against parliamentary self-government, opposed the Congress, and sought an ‘Anglo-Muslim alliance’, becoming the originator of the  two-nation theory  — the doctrine that Hindus and Muslims form two distinct nations. The Urdu-Hindi controversy, his dependence on government funding for the Aligarh college, and rising Hindu revivalism all accelerated the transition. 6. Conclusion.  Sir Syed was a genuine modernizer who dragged a defeated and conservative community toward science, English education and social reform. But his later communal politics laid the ideological seed of Partition, so that his educational legacy at Aligarh and his political legacy in the two-nation theory pull in exactly opposite directions. Q — Analyse Sri Aurobindo’s theory of cultural/spiritual nationalism, his conception of Swaraj and his idea of freedom. (UPSC 2017/2016/2014/2013) What it’s asking:  Three linked ideas — the nation as spirit, Swaraj as complete independence, and freedom as inner self-realisation. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Nationalism as spirituality  — he ‘connected nationalism with spirituality’;  Romain Rolland  saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’.  (Nationalism is not a political programme but a way of life like religion — the patriot is a devotee, not a party worker.) 2. Cultural/spiritual nationalism  — ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the  nation is a faith, a religion, the nation has a spirit ’.  (Herder’s national spirit + Bankim’s Mother India as Goddess + Vivekananda’s Neo-Vedanta — India’s ‘divine mission’ is to give spirituality to the world.) 3. Passive resistance  — in his extremist phase he rejected Moderate constitutionalism and theorised organised resistance.  (Swadeshi, boycott and non-cooperation — the doctrinal ground on which Gandhi’s Satyagraha was later built.) 4. Swaraj as Purna Swaraj  — the first to read Swaraj as  complete independence .  (‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’; to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’.) 5. Inner freedom  — the liberal view is ‘mechanical’ and the socialist neglects the individual; true freedom is  inner freedom .  (‘Obeying the law of our own existence’ — swadharma — so a man free of foreign rule but enslaved to his appetites is not free.) 6. Conclusion  — he raised nationalism from programme to vocation, though critics call it reactionary and idealistic.  (By rooting it in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma he radicalised the freedom movement.) Model Answer 1. Nationalism as spirituality.  Sri Aurobindo  ‘connected nationalism with spirituality’, and  Romain Rolland  saw in him ‘the highest synthesis of the genius of Asia and of Europe’. For him nationalism was not a mere political programme but a way of life like religion: the patriot approaches the nation as a devotee approaches the divine, with faith and self-surrender rather than a calculation of interest. This converted the freedom struggle from a constitutional claim into a spiritual vocation. 2. Cultural / spiritual nationalism.  Applying the German romantic idea —  Herder’s  claim that ‘the nation is natural and has a spirit’ — and drawing on  Bankim’s  vision of  Mother India as Goddess  and  Vivekananda’s  Neo-Vedanta, Aurobindo held that ‘the nation is not a piece of land… the  nation is a faith, the nation is a religion, the nation has a spirit ’. India is not a territory but a living Mother with a  divine mission  — to give spirituality to a materialist world — so her subjection is a spiritual and not merely a political wrong. 3. Passive resistance.  In his extremist phase Aurobindo dismissed the Moderates’ constitutional petitioning as futile and pioneered a systematic theory of  passive resistance  — organised non-cooperation with an alien administration, backed by swadeshi, boycott and national education, to be abandoned only if repression made resistance impossible. This body of doctrine prepared the ground on which  Gandhi’s  Satyagraha would be built a decade later. 4. Swaraj as Purna Swaraj.  He was the first Indian leader to interpret Swaraj as  Purna Swaraj  — complete independence rather than colonial self-government within the Empire — to be won through swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance. ‘Political freedom is the life-breath of a nation’, he wrote, and to attempt social reform ‘without aiming first at political freedom is the height of ignorance’. Swaraj is thus the ‘necessary condition for India to accomplish its destined goal’ — the political shell within which the spiritual mission can be realised. 5. Inner freedom.  Aurobindo found the liberal, near-anarchic conception of liberty ‘mechanical’ — an absence of external restraint that says nothing about what the free man becomes — and the socialist conception neglectful of the individual. Real freedom is  inner freedom : ‘obeying the law of our own existence’, that is, swadharma. A man released from foreign rule but enslaved to his own appetites has not become free. His later thought —  Sacchidananda, the Supermind and Integral Yoga  — accordingly makes national self-realisation one stage in the spiritual evolution of humanity as a whole. 6. Conclusion.  Aurobindo raised nationalism from a political programme to a spiritual vocation. Critics call his spiritual nationalism reactionary, idealistic and open to majoritarian appropriation; yet by rooting freedom in an ‘open and universal’ Sanatana Dharma rather than a narrow creed, and by demanding Purna Swaraj when others asked only for reform, he decisively radicalised the Indian freedom movement. Q — Evaluate Ambedkar’s idea of social justice — annihilation of caste, critique of Hinduism and of Marxism, and his conception of social/economic/political democracy — comparing his egalitarian justice with Rawls. (UPSC 2022/2020/2018/2016/2013) What it’s asking:  Build Ambedkar’s theory of justice upward from caste, then measure it against Rawls’ procedural justice. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Annihilation of caste  — caste is ‘not the division of labour but the  division of labourers ’, held together by  endogamy .  (A guild you may leave; a caste you are born into and must marry within — so inter-caste marriage, not ritual reform, is the real solvent.) 2. Critique of Hinduism  — ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, sanctified by the Vedas and the Manusmriti.  (He would ‘put dynamite’ on the Manusmriti, and finding reform impossible from within, converted to Buddhism in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’.) 3. The three democracies  — democracy is ‘a way of life’ on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’; political democracy must be completed by  social and economic democracy .  (One man one vote is worthless if the same man may not draw water from the village well.) 4. Constitutional morality  — the safeguard, alongside ‘state socialism’.  (Not merely obeying the text but internalising its spirit — self-restraint, due process, respect for dissent — in a soil he called ‘essentially undemocratic’.) 5. Critique of Marxism  — religion is not mere ‘opium’, and ‘society is more exploitative than the state’.  (Buddhism, built on karuna, samata and prajna, liberates; and the untouchable is humiliated by his neighbours, so the state must be his instrument of emancipation, not his enemy.) 6. Ambedkar vs Rawls & conclusion  — his justice is  egalitarian and outcome-oriented ; Rawls’ is  procedural .  (Rawls reasons from a hypothetical veil of ignorance; Ambedkar starts from a real history of humiliation and demands safeguards to undo it.) Model Answer 1. Annihilation of caste.  Ambedkar  — ‘chief architect of the Constitution’ and himself born a Mahar — made the  annihilation of caste  his central concern. In  Annihilation of Caste  he argues that caste is ‘not the division of labour but the  division of labourers ’: a guild divides work and may be left, whereas caste divides human beings themselves into fixed, graded compartments one is born into. Its steel frame is  endogamy , which is why he held that inter-caste marriage and inter-dining, not the reform of ritual, are the real solvents of the system. 2. Critique of Hinduism.  Caste for Ambedkar is not an excrescence but the essence: ‘Hinduism is nothing but Brahmanism’, a graded inequality sanctified by the Vedas and above all by the  Manusmriti , on which he said he would ‘put dynamite’ and which he publicly burnt in 1927. Because the sanction is scriptural, reform from within is impossible — destroy belief in the sanctity of the shastras and caste collapses. Finding no such reform forthcoming, he  converted to Buddhism  in 1956: ‘I reject the religion which treats me as inferior’. 3. The three democracies.  For Ambedkar democracy is not a form of government but ‘a way of life’, resting on the ‘inseparable trinity of liberty, equality and fraternity’, which he traced to the Buddha rather than to the French Revolution. Hence his warning that India was entering a life of contradictions: political equality of one man one vote alongside social and economic inequality. Political democracy must therefore be completed by  social and economic democracy , for ‘political democracy cannot last unless there lies at its base social democracy’ — the vote is empty if the voter may not draw water from the village well. 4. Constitutional morality.  The instruments of that completion are  constitutional morality  and ‘state socialism’. Borrowing the phrase from Grote, Ambedkar meant not mere obedience to the constitutional text but internalisation of its spirit — self-restraint by those in power, respect for forms and for dissent, and the settling of conflict by due process rather than agitation — a habit he thought had to be deliberately cultivated because Indian soil was ‘essentially undemocratic’. Alongside it he urged state ownership of key industries and of land, so that concentrated economic power could not defeat formal equality. 5. Critique of Marxism.  Ambedkar rejected two Marxist claims. First, that religion is mere ‘opium’: Buddhism, resting on karuna, samata and prajna, is a liberating morality and not a narcotic. Second, that the state is the chief instrument of oppression — for Ambedkar ‘society is more exploitative than the state’, since the untouchable is humiliated by his own neighbours and not primarily by officials, so the state must be strengthened as an instrument of emancipation. He also rejected violent revolution and the dictatorship of the proletariat in favour of constitutional methods. 6. Ambedkar vs Rawls & conclusion.  Ambedkar’s social justice is  egalitarian and outcome-oriented  — the active uplift of the depressed classes through state action, reservation and constitutional safeguards — whereas  Rawls’  ‘justice as fairness’ is  procedural , derived from a hypothetical original position behind a veil of ignorance. Ambedkar begins not from an abstraction but from a documented history of humiliation. He thus transformed justice in India from a matter of procedure into one of  substantive social emancipation , making the annihilation of caste and the completion of democracy his enduring legacy. Q — Trace M.N. Roy’s ideational journey from Marxism to Radical Humanism, and identify the major components of Modern Indian Political Thought with reference to Gandhi and Roy. What it’s asking:  Follow Roy’s three phases and his two breaks, then use Gandhi and Roy together to name what modern Indian thought is made of. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Three phases  —  nationalism → communism → radical humanism .  (A revolutionary who founded the CPI abroad and ended by dissolving his own party for the sake of the individual.) 2. Break with Lenin  — at the Comintern (1920) his  Supplementary Theses  opposed Lenin’s two-stage strategy.  (Lenin wanted communists to ally with bourgeois-nationalists like the Congress; Roy insisted they lead the colonial proletariat directly — ‘for socialism to win in the West it must first win in the East’.) 3. Critique of Marxism  — it  subdues individualism  in ‘the collective ego of the proletariat’; historical materialism is ‘economic determinism’; the sanction against exploitation is ‘not economic but  moral ’.  (Marxism is ‘more method than dogma’.) 4. Radical Humanism  —  New Humanism: A Manifesto  rests on  Reason, Morality and Freedom .  (Man, not class or party, is the measure — freedom is ‘the progressive removal of restrictions on the unfolding of the potentialities of individuals… not as cogs in a mechanized social organism’.) 5. Party-less radical democracy  — parties ‘bred social and political immorality’ and reduce sovereignty to a ‘legal fiction’.  (He dissolved his own party in 1948 for ‘people’s committees’ and ‘miniature republics’ — candidates chosen for merit, not for a party ticket.) 6. Gandhi & Roy — and conclusion  — spiritual against rationalist, yet both converge on  decentralisation, the individual, and morality in politics .  (Bidyut Chakraborty thinks Roy never fully escaped Marxism, yet his is the most individual-centred voice in modern Indian thought.) Model Answer 1. Three phases.  M.N. Roy’s  intellectual life moved through three distinct phases —  nationalism → communism → radical humanism . Beginning as a revolutionary nationalist in Bengal, he became a founder of the Communist Party of India and one of the very few Asians to hold a leading position in the Comintern, and ended by dissolving his own party in the name of the individual — a trajectory from collective revolution to personal freedom. 2. Break with Lenin.  The first break came at the Second Congress of the Comintern (1920), where Roy clashed with  Lenin . Lenin’s colonial theses proposed a two-stage strategy in which communists would first ally with bourgeois-nationalist movements such as the Congress; Roy’s  Supplementary Theses  replied that such movements were led by classes with a stake in the existing order, and that communists must organise and lead the colonial proletariat and peasantry directly. His larger claim was that imperial profit sustained European capitalism, so that ‘for socialism to win in the West it must first win in the East’. 3. Critique of Marxism.  Disillusioned, Roy came to regard ‘Marxism as more method than dogma’ and criticised it on three counts. It  subdues individualism , dissolving the person into ‘the collective ego of the proletariat’ and then into the party. Its historical materialism is mere ‘economic determinism’, denying the creative role of ideas and of human will in history. And the true sanction for ending exploitation is ‘not economic but  moral ’ — a revolution begun in immorality cannot end in freedom. 4. Radical Humanism.  His alternative, set out in  New Humanism: A Manifesto  and the  Twenty-Two Theses , rests on three elements.  Reason  — man is essentially rational, and blind faith, whether religious or ideological, must be rejected.  Morality  — secular and rational, rooted in man’s own rationality rather than in divine command. And  Freedom , defined as ‘the progressive removal of all restrictions on the unfolding of the potentialities of individuals… not as cogs in a mechanized social organism’. Man, not class or party, is the measure of every social arrangement, and the goal is a cosmopolitan ‘commonwealth of spiritually free men’. 5. Party-less radical democracy.  Holding that the party system ‘bred social and political immorality’ — subordinating conscience to the whip and reducing popular sovereignty to a ‘legal fiction’ exercised for a moment at the ballot box — Roy dissolved his own party in 1948 in favour of ‘organized democracy’: decentralised ‘people’s committees’ and ‘miniature republics’ in which candidates are chosen for personal merit rather than a party ticket, and power is exercised continuously from below with primacy given to the individual. 6. Gandhi & Roy — and conclusion.  The major components of modern Indian political thought are visible in the contrast between the two.  Gandhi  is spiritual, treats religion as a moralising force, and looks to a decentralised Ram Rajya secured by non-violence;  Roy  is rationalist and humanist, militantly secular, individual-centred and party-less. Yet both converge on  decentralisation, the primacy of the individual and the community, and the insistence on morality in politics  — the recurring signature of modern Indian thought. Though  Bidyut Chakraborty  judged Roy ‘unable to free himself entirely from Marxism’, his radical humanism remains its most genuinely individual-centred and cosmopolitan voice.
